title: Stop Scanning 400-Row Tables: The Flamegraph Hiding in Your Metrics
summary: Render hierarchical metrics as interactive flamegraphs in Grafana core panel. No plugin: the frame contract, the transforms, and the traps that fail silently.
body_text: The dashboard is telling you something is wrong. Traffic to one region is up. Error counts are climbing somewhere you can't see yet, and a cluster is filling toward its limit. You open the breakdown to find the culprit, and you get what you always get: a table. Four hundred rows of region, service, endpoint, and a number. Sorted by that number, if you're lucky. So you start scanning. Row by row, holding the shape of the tree in your head, trying to remember whether checkout in us-east was the big one or whether that was search in eu-west. The information is all there. That table hides something: your metric isn't flat, it's a tree. And there's a visualization built for trees that turns " scan four hundred rows " into " look at the widest bar ." The busiest path becomes the widest thing on the screen; the workload quietly eating your cluster becomes impossible to miss. It's called a flamegraph. You've probably only ever seen one profiling CPU. A table is the wrong shape for a hierarchy Flamegraphs might be the best data visualization nobody lets you use. Profilers worked this out a long time ago: stack a set of nested bars, size each one by its total, and your eye goes straight to the widest. No reading. No scanning. But you have hierarchy all over your metrics. Request traffic by region → service → endpoint. Storage by cluster → namespace → volume. Memory by zone → nodepool → namespace → workload. Anything with a natural nesting is a flamegraph waiting to happen, and you're staring at it as a 400-row table instead. The flamegraph panel doesn't care where the data comes from Rendering a flamegraph doesn't need a plugin. Grafana has shipped a real, interactive flamegraph panel in core since v10.1, and we ran this exact setup on 10.1, 11.1, 12.4, and 13.1 - the same frame renders on every one. It was built for Pyroscope, but the panel itself is indifferent to the source: feed it any datasource frame that matches its contract and it renders a zoomable, click-to-focus flamegraph. So you can point it at a plain PromQL query over a hierarchical metric and get the real thing. Here's how, including the handful of things that will cost you an afternoon if nobody warns you. What you want to see Say you have http_requests_total with three hierarchy labels: ‍ region = us-east | eu-west | ap-south service = checkout | search | profile | ... endpoint = /cart | /pay | /query | ... You want the root to be all traffic, then a level per label: region, then service, then endpoint. Click the widest bar and everything outside that subtree falls away. The recipe is the same for any hierarchy; the version we run is four levels deep. The contract the panel actually enforces The panel reads exactly one table frame, data.series[0], and it matches fields by field.name, not display name. Hold onto that; it's the source of the most infuriating error below. It wants four fields: ← Scroll to see more → Field Type Meaning level number Depth in the hierarchy (0 = root). label string The node name shown on the bar. value number Total for this node and its subtree. self number Amount attributed to this node alone. ‍ The one non-obvious rule: rows must be in depth-first pre-order (nested-set order), every node immediately followed by its entire subtree. That falls out of the paths themselves: each non-root node's path is a strict prefix of its descendants', so sorting by path reproduces the order. Get the order wrong and the bars come out as nonsense widths even though every number in the table is correct, which is the worst kind of bug to chase. Good news on self: set it to 0 everywhere. The flame widths are driven entirely by value , so unless you want the "self time" shading, self = 0 is fine. Building the frame from a hierarchical metric Two halves: a query that emits the right rows, and a transform chain that shapes them into the frame. Start with the query. You emit one instant, format=table query that or -unions a root row with one row-set per level. Each term produces just three columns, {level, label, path} , using nothing but stock PromQL: label_replace and label_join . The one function you'll reach for that PromQL doesn't obviously have is "set a label to a constant." The idiom is label_replace(v, "dst", "constant", "", "") : an empty source label and empty regex match every series, so it stamps dst = "constant" on all of them. That's the pure-PromQL stand-in for MetricsQL's label_set , and it works right down to setting the control-byte sentinel (<SEP> below, the empty-value guard explained in trap #3): ‍ The middle levels are the same shape, summing by region alone, then by region, service . Wrapping each term in sum by(level,label,path)(...) is doing real work: it throws away every other label, so the frame comes back with only those three columns instead of dragging the raw dimensions along. Now the transforms. All built-in: labelsToFields → merge → convertFieldType(level → number) → calculateField(value = Value * 1) # creates a field literally named "value" → calculateField(self = Value - Value) # self = 0; widths come from value → sortBy(path asc) # this IS the depth-first ordering → organize(exclude Time, Value, path) That's the whole thing. The sortBy(path asc) step is the entire depth-first ordering trick; trap #4 explains why the separator matters. One note if you're on VictoriaMetrics: MetricsQL gives you label_set(v, "dst", "constant") as a tidier shorthand for that label_replace(..., "", "") dance. The query above stays in stock PromQL on purpose, so it runs unchanged on plain Prometheus, and both forms produce byte-for-byte the same frame. That's the technique. The rest is knowing where it breaks. The six traps that fail silently The chart looks fine until it isn't. They're in the order they'll bite you, and the first two are the killers. 1. organize's rename doesn't do what you think. It sets config.displayName, not field.name, and the panel matches on field.name. So you rename your columns to level/label/value/self in organize, the table preview looks perfect, and the panel still throws "Data is missing fields." The fix is baked into the recipe: name level/label/path in the query, and mint value/self with calculateField, which (unlike organize) sets a real field.name. 2. An instant format=table query returns one frame per series. This is the big one. Those level/label/path values don't come back as table columns; they ride as labels on the value field of each single-row frame. The panel only reads series[0], so without labelsToFields → merge up front it sees one lonely series and gives up. Don't trust a glance at Explore or a Table panel to tell you what the flamegraph sees: what you're looking at there is the response after Grafana's frontend has reshaped it into a table, and the panel works off the raw shape. The verify step below shows you that raw shape. 3. Prometheus and VictoriaMetrics both drop empty label values. So your carefully built root row with path="" evaporates, and any node with an empty dimension goes with it. Now you have frames with mismatched schemas, and merge quietly produces garbage. Two fixes, both in the recipe: make the root path a sentinel byte (we use \x1f, ASCII unit separator), and map empty nodes to (untagged) with label_replace(v, "label", "(untagged)", "label", ""). The sentinel survives the round trip (it comes back JSON-encoded as ), which is the point: it's non-empty, so it isn't dropped. 4. Depth-first order means sorting by path ascending. Using \x1f as the separator between path segments is deliberate: it sorts below every letter, digit, and dash, so no sibling's subtree can interleave with another's, and the root row (whose path is the lone sentinel) sorts first. This is also why a "nice" separator like / or . will bite you the moment an identifier contains one. 5. You can't persist "full-width, flame-only, and clickable" all at once. The showFlameGraphOnly option gives the flame the whole width but kills click-to-focus, and it's undocumented: no control in the panel editor, settable only in the dashboard JSON. The live in-panel view toggle ("Top Table / Flame Graph / Both") is a different switch. Flip it to "Flame Graph" and you keep the full-width flame and click-to-zoom, but that choice isn't saved. (The gate is {!showFlameGraphOnly} in the flamegraph component source; there's no persisted selectedView option. In the default "Both" mode the table sits beside the flame past ~800px.) 6. Whether the panel respects your unit depends on the Grafana version. This is the one place the versions diverge. On 10.1 and 11.1, the flamegraph ignores the field's unit entirely: it labels everything Count and shows the raw number ("1.98 Tri samples"), so a memory chart reads as if you're counting samples. Unit support landed later; by 12.4 and 13.1 it honors the field, so set the unit to bytes and the flame and its table format as TiB/MiB (with 0 B selves). Everything else is identical across all four versions: the frame contract, the transforms, the DFS ordering, the sentinel. How to verify without guessing The transforms run client-side , which has an annoying consequence: you can't validate the final frame by hitting the datasource API, because the API only ever hands you the raw series, never the post-transform result. What you can do, and what we'd recommend as step one every time, is POST your query to /api/ds/query, the exact endpoint the panel uses, and read the frames it returns. That tells you the two things that matter. You'll see the one-frame-per-series shape from trap #2, with level/label/path sitting in each value field's labels. And you'll see there's no value or self column yet, so you know exactly which transforms you still owe the panel. It turns "why is it erroring" into something you can just look at. Since that's the pre-transform view, confirm the final result by rendering the panel and looking at it. If you want a proper unit test of the transform chain for CI, replay it headlessly with @grafana/data: register the standard transformers, run transformDataFrame, and assert on the field names the panel checks. But for day-to-day work, "inspect the raw frame, then render it" catches everything. Where to take it next You can push the hierarchy out of the query and make it configurable from the dashboard: enumerate your dimension names into a query variable per level, give each level an exclusion regex that references the ones above it, and Grafana re-evaluates the chain whenever an upstream variable changes. One dashboard then gives you any ordering on the fly, region → service today and service → region tomorrow. Treat that as a direction, not a validated recipe; the core technique is everything above it. The widest bar is always the next thing to look at A hierarchy in a table is something nobody reads. As a flamegraph, the same numbers answer your question before you've finished scrolling. No plugin required: just the frame contract, about six transforms, and the six traps above, enough to skip the afternoon this cost us. So the next time the dashboard goes red, the row that matters won't be hiding on line two hundred of a table. It's the first bar you see.

title: How to move USD to MXN from Chase to Banamex
summary: Options for moving business funds from Chase to Banamex: SWIFT, bank FX, USD accounts, SPID where available, and Coba direct debit to SPEI.
body_text: If your logistics or transport company keeps dollars at Chase and needs to pay people in Mexico through Banamex, the question is not only can I send the money? It is which route gives me the right timing, proof, FX control, and operational visibility? For companies moving freight, paying carriers, funding suppliers, or covering expenses in Mexico, the same payment can be handled several ways. Some are bank-native. Some require phone calls or treasury work. Coba is built for the recurring operating flow: pull USD from your existing US bank account when supported, convert USD to MXN, and pay out locally in Mexico by SPEI. The common situation A US-side company has USD available at Chase. The Mexico-side obligation is in pesos at Banamex: supplier invoices, customs-related services, yard expenses, carrier payments, payroll support, taxes, or urgent operating costs. Chase is a common US business banking starting point for companies that pay vendors, subsidiaries, or operating teams in Mexico. It is not border-specific, but many finance teams already use it for ACH, wires, and treasury workflows. Banamex, also searched as Citibanamex, remains a major commercial banking destination in Mexico for business accounts, treasury, payroll, and supplier payments. The right path depends on whether the recipient needs MXN immediately, whether you need a clean comprobante, whether the amount is recurring, and whether your team wants to keep the existing bank relationship without running every payment manually. Option 1: send a SWIFT wire from Chase to Banamex For a larger or one-off payment, a traditional international wire can make sense. Your team can ask Chase for the correct process to send funds to Mexico and ask Banamex for the beneficiary instructions. Common variations: Send USD by SWIFT to a Mexican bank account that can receive USD, if the account is eligible. Send USD and let the receiving bank handle conversion to MXN, if that is how the account is configured. Send MXN directly if the US bank offers an FX wire or peso payment service. What to check before using this route: Does the beneficiary account at Banamex receive USD, MXN, or both? Does the payment require a SWIFT code, intermediary bank, CLABE, account number, or special reference? Who sets the FX rate and when is it locked? What are the sending, intermediary, and receiving fees? What happens if a reference is missing or the receiving bank needs extra compliance information? This route can work, but it is often heavier than necessary for recurring operational payments. Option 2: ask Chase to handle the currency exchange Some US banks can help business customers convert USD to MXN before sending funds to Mexico. Depending on the bank and the account setup, this can involve an online wire flow, an international banking desk, or a phone-assisted FX payment. This can be useful when your team wants the recipient to receive pesos directly. The tradeoff is that the process may be less automated, the FX spread may be embedded in the rate, and the operational proof may live across emails, wire confirmations, and bank portals. Before choosing this route, ask: Can Chase send MXN to Banamex, or only USD? Is the rate visible before approval? Can the payment be repeated with saved beneficiaries? What cutoff applies for same-day processing? Can your team export the receipt and reconcile it against invoices? Option 3: send USD to a Mexican USD account Some Mexican business accounts can receive USD, usually under specific eligibility rules and documentation. If the recipient has a USD-capable account at Banamex, a US company may be able to send USD and let the Mexico-side business decide when to convert. This can help when the recipient manages USD costs or wants to control conversion timing. It can also add steps: the recipient may still need to convert internally to MXN before sending SPEI payments to employees, vendors, or other Mexican beneficiaries. Use this route only after confirming the account details directly with Banamex. Do not assume that every CLABE receives USD. Option 4: SPID or USD flows inside Mexico SPID is Mexico’s interbank USD payment system for eligible legal entities and participating banks. It can matter when both sides in Mexico operate with USD accounts. For the Chase to Banamex scenario, SPID is usually not the first step from the US bank. It becomes relevant after dollars are already inside Mexico and the Mexican company wants to move USD between eligible Mexican bank accounts or then convert using its bank’s own services. The important point: SPID availability is bank and account specific. Ask Banamex whether the account supports USD receipts, SPID, internal conversion, and MXN payout workflows. Option 5: use Coba direct debit to SPEI For recurring business payments from USD to MXN, Coba can be the operational layer around the banks you already use. A typical flow looks like this: Connect or authorize your existing US bank account, such as Chase, where supported. Pull USD into the Coba flow using direct debit or another supported funding method. Convert USD to MXN. Send MXN locally in Mexico by SPEI to Banamex or another Mexican bank. Keep payment status, beneficiary details, and receipts in one operating workflow. This is especially useful when the job is not a one-time treasury transfer, but a repeated operating need: paying suppliers, drivers, customs-related vendors, yards, payroll support, or urgent expenses in Mexico. A recommendation from operators who have lived this Do not build your cross-border operation around only one money route. Even if you never use Coba, your company is safer when you have two, three, or four practical ways to move money from USD to MXN. Sometimes the best route is the fastest route. Sometimes it is the route with the best FX rate. Sometimes it is the one that gives your team automation, receipts, and less follow-up work. Banks can have cutoffs, compliance questions, portal issues, or a relationship manager who is out of office. When your logistics operation still needs to pay carriers, vendors, customs-related providers, or operating teams in Mexico, optionality matters. That is why many companies keep more than one path available: a bank wire path, a bank FX path, a Mexico-side USD/SPID path where eligible, and an automated operating path such as Coba. It lets your team choose based on the job: speed, rate, reliability, proof, or automation. Why companies use Coba for the repeatable flow Customers use Coba because they can get to a reliable USD to MXN operating flow quickly and keep using it without turning every payment into a manual bank project. A few cents of FX negotiation can matter on the right transaction, but sometimes the bigger cost is the operational drag: waiting on someone, re-entering instructions, chasing receipts, reconciling payments, or worrying whether the money will arrive in time. For recurring logistics payments, the value is not only the exchange rate. It is having a process your team can trust when the work has to get done. Plan your pesos before the deadline The easiest USD to MXN conversion is the one you do not have to rush. If you know you will have obligations in Mexican pesos, try to keep enough MXN available to cover them before the due date. Planning ahead gives you more control over timing, rates, and routing. Last-minute conversions are where problems tend to appear: bank cutoffs, missing beneficiary details, FX approvals, compliance reviews, or urgent supplier pressure. Of course, logistics operations do not always allow perfect planning. Trucks move, loads change, invoices arrive late, and urgent expenses happen. That is one reason Coba exists: to give companies a cleaner fallback and recurring route when the operation cannot wait. Which route should you use? Use a traditional SWIFT or bank FX flow when: The amount is large and one-time. Your treasury team wants everything handled inside the bank. The recipient has verified SWIFT and USD/MXN receiving instructions. Use a USD account or SPID-related route when: The Mexican company has eligible USD accounts. The recipient wants to hold dollars in Mexico. Both sides have confirmed the bank-specific process. Use Coba when: You need a repeatable USD to MXN operating flow. You want to keep using your current US bank but avoid manual payment work every time. Your Mexican beneficiaries need MXN by SPEI. You care about status, comprobantes, reconciliation, and after-hours operational continuity. A simple way to think about it Chase and Banamex can both be good banks. The problem for logistics companies is that cross-border operations do not always fit neatly into bank cutoffs, manual FX calls, wire references, and back-office reconciliation. If your team is regularly moving USD to MXN for business payments in Mexico, you do not need to replace your bank relationship to improve the workflow. You need a cleaner operating layer between the US bank balance and the Mexican SPEI payment. Explore Coba USD/MXN business payments or start an application . If you want to compare your current Chase to Banamex process first, book a short discovery call . This article is educational. Bank products, fees, SWIFT instructions, USD accounts, SPID availability, cutoffs, and FX spreads can change. Confirm details with your bank before sending funds.

title: Why does a removed user show as inactive instead of being deleted, and what does that preserve in the history?
summary: Understand why a removed user shows as inactive instead of being deleted in Jestor, and what that preserves in the history.
body_text: In Jestor , removing a user doesn't delete them from the system: their status changes to inactive, specifically to preserve the history of everything that person changed on records in the past. Why this logic exists If a user were completely deleted, the entire history of actions they performed — such as changes to cards, approvals, and record updates — would lose its reference to who did what. By keeping the user as inactive, Jestor guarantees that any entry in the history correctly continues to show that person was responsible for a given change, even though they no longer have access to the account. Status What it means Active User with normal access to the account Inactive Removed user, no access, but with history preserved How to check inactive users Go to the user management area. Use the status filter to view only inactive, active, or all users. Confirm that inactive users are exactly the ones removed earlier. Check the table's history to see actions performed by those users in the past. Why choose Jestor Intact history : no change loses its authorship reference, even after a user is removed. Clear management filters : you can quickly view just the active ones, just the inactive ones, or everyone. Reorganized visuals : the user management area also works in dark mode. Can an inactive user access the account again? No. Inactive status means the user was removed and no longer has access; only their action history remains recorded. Can you see how many inactive users an account has? Yes, the status filter lets you see exactly how many users are inactive, active, or any other status. Does an inactive user still occupy a seat in the account? The user management area shows the count of available seats, which helps track account usage as users are removed or added. Reference video Check out more hands-on tutorials on the Jestor YouTube channel. Get to know Jestor With Jestor, you can automate workflows, connect teams, and build internal systems your way — all without code and powered by AI. Discover Jestor at jestor.com and see how to take your company's operations to a new level of efficiency and control.

title: Make Yourself Redundant: Why I'm Optimistic About AI and the Future of Data People
summary: The best data careers won't belong to the people who resist AI. They'll belong to the ones who use it to finally do the work they never had time for. A case for optimism, from one data team's CEO.
body_text: A while back, another CEO gave me one of those pieces of advice that doesn't land at first and then won't leave you alone. He said: "Your job as a CEO is to make yourself redundant for your company. And you'll fail at it every single day." His point was simple. Everything I personally do is, by definition, a bottleneck. The company depends on me to do it, which means it can't move faster than me on that thing. So my real job is to give it away: to empower other people, to build systems, to make sure the company doesn't need me for as much as possible. But why is this doomed to fail? Because every time I succeed in offloading something, I create capacity in myself to take on something I never had time for before. The bottleneck just moves. I become more valuable, not less, because my output keeps growing. I will never actually finish making myself redundant. The list of things only I can do gets shorter on one end and longer on the other, forever. I keep thinking about this advice because I think it's a healthy way to talk about what AI is doing to data teams right now. The discomfort is real. So is the opportunity. There's an uncomfortable feeling in the air for a lot of data people I talk to. The sense that the ground is shifting under you faster than you can keep up. I'm not going to pretend that feeling is wrong. An inspiring Israeli president once said: "Optimists and pessimists die the same way. They just live differently ". The change is real, and it's inevitable. The pessimists obsess about "will AI replace me?", but the optimists should focus on the more useful question, the same one that founder asked me: What will you do with the capacity you get back? Because if you're a data person reading this, I'd bet two things are true about you right now. One: you're underwater. You have too much on your plate. I meet teams who tell me about projects that span one or two years. Not because the projects are that hard, but because there are only so many hours in a sprint and only so many sprints in a quarter. What if those projects could ship in a quarter? What if your two-week sprint could be done in a day? What if the tedious manual work, the broken pipeline at 2am, the documentation nobody has time to write, the test coverage you keep meaning to get to, was just... handled? Two: there's a version of your job you've never gotten to do. There are things you've wanted to build for the business but written off as impossible, not because they were technically hard but because you didn't have the people. You could build a beautiful finance data model. But you couldn't assign a financial analyst to every single employee making budget decisions. You could build great dashboards. But you couldn't sit next to every PM and help them interpret the numbers in their specific context. There was always a ceiling on how far your work could reach, and that ceiling was headcount. That ceiling is coming down. And the backlog? That's shrinking too. Human intelligence used to be the bottleneck for a huge category of data work. It's not anymore. At least not for the repetitive, well-scoped, executional parts. Where human intelligence is still very much the bottleneck is in designing intelligent systems : figuring out what to build, deciding how the pieces fit, encoding the business logic and the guardrails, choosing what's worth automating and what isn't. That, to me, is the actual job description for data people going forward. Designing the intelligent systems that leverage data, and building the data platform that powers them. It's more interesting work. It's more ambitious work. It's more impactful work. The same president also said: “We should use our imagination more than our memory”. This is what’s required of data people today. Imagine what can be done, forget that it was impossible until recently. What we're building at Elementary We're going all in on one idea: the experience of having extra data engineers on your team. Not "an AI that helps you." A team. Agents that take ownership of tasks, do the work, and bring it back to you for review. You stop being the person doing every manual task and start being the person managing a team that does them for you. You go from individual contributor to a tech lead overnight, except your team never sleeps and never gets bored doing repetitive work. The point isn't to remove you from the loop. It's to put you in a different position in the loop. You set the standards. You review the work. You decide what's worth building. The agents handle the parts of the job that were burning your hours without growing your skills. If the last decade of data tools was about giving you better instruments to do the work yourself, this future is about giving you a team to do the work for you. And it doesn't stop with data people Here's something we didn't fully expect, but is now one of the most exciting parts of what's happening: The biggest adoption of our agents isn't coming from data engineers. It's coming from business users. People who have always had questions about the data, always had ideas for what they wanted to track, always had small changes they needed made but were blocked by not knowing SQL, not knowing to code, not knowing the infra. So they'd file a ticket. Wait two weeks. Get something close to what they asked for. File another ticket. Those people can now complete end-to-end data tasks on their own. Not because they suddenly learned to code, but because they don't need to. They can describe what they want and an agent can do it within the standards and guardrails the data team has set. This is the thing self-service data promised and never really delivered. Not because the idea was wrong, but because the interface was always still some version of "here's a tool, now learn it." The new interface is just: tell someone what you need. For data teams, this changes the relationship completely. You stop being a service desk. You start being the people who design the system that lets the whole company work with data directly. You become more leveraged, not less. So, back to the original advice Make yourself redundant. You'll fail at it every day. The version of your job that AI can do, that's the version you should want to give up. Not because your job is going away, but because the more of that you offload, the more space you have for the work that actually requires you. The strategic calls. The system design. The judgment about what's worth building. The relationships with the business. That's the future we're building Elementary for. Not a smaller role for data people. A bigger one. ‍

title: Best ERP Software for Life Sciences
summary: General ERP rarely understands samples, aliquots, instrument runs, or chain of custody. Scispot is life sciences ERP for the lab: native ops plus connections to SAP, NetSuite, Dynamics, and other enterprise systems.
body_text: ERP Software for Life Sciences: Why Scispot is the lab-native ERP for biotech, pharma, CRO, diagnostic, and medical device teams Faster time to market. Greater efficiency. Less expense. Simpler regulatory compliance. These are practical goals for manufacturers in the life sciences industry and for the labs that support them, but they are hard to reach when work moves through siloed operating systems, spreadsheets, local files, inboxes, and disconnected lab apps. ERP software enables life sciences companies to replace that fragmentation with one system that centrally manages all business processes, from accounting to inventory. The problem is that a general ERP rarely understands a sample, aliquot, plate, instrument run, protocol version, quality result, or chain of custody. Scispot fills that gap. It is life sciences ERP software for the lab, and it works as an ERP solution by managing the scientific resources and day-to-day operations that determine whether a company can deliver. It then connects that work to finance, procurement, CRM, and supply chain systems. For many biotech, CRO, diagnostic, bioprocessing, and medical device teams, Scispot can become the primary operations ERP used inside the lab. Larger companies can run Scispot beside SAP, Oracle NetSuite, Microsoft Dynamics 365, Odoo, QuickBooks, Salesforce, or another enterprise system. The result is a single source of truth for lab inventory, samples, methods, instruments, workflows, quality controls, approvals, reports, and customer delivery, without forcing the company to replace systems that still work. This guide answers: What is ERP software? What is ERP software for life sciences? What is a life sciences ERP? What are the key features of a life sciences ERP? What are the benefits of ERP software for life sciences? It also explains how Scispot supports native lab operations while connecting to existing ERP systems. ‍ ‍ What is ERP software? Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) software is a comprehensive suite of integrated business applications that helps organizations automate and integrate their core business processes. ERP software centralizes data and operating information so people get real-time insight into back- and front-office activities instead of waiting for teams to reconcile separate systems. Typical ERP scope includes Manufacturing/Shop Floor, Inventory, Material Resource Planning (MRP), Financial Processes, Supplier Documentation, Data and Communications, Sales Activities, and Customer Data and Interactions (CRM). In a conventional company, these functions connect purchasing, production, sales, finance, suppliers, customers, and reporting. Most modern ERP software solutions are deployed via the web and use Cloud-based platforms because they support easier implementation and scalability, easier collaboration between multiple locations or departments, and the ability to automate workflows and dynamically update data across applications. That model works well for common business records. Life science companies need more because the operating record also includes scientific context, material lineage, instrument data, methods, quality checks, and regulated approvals. Scispot brings those lab-specific records into the ERP model. Its native apps include ELN++ , LIMS++ , SDMS++, GLUE , Smart Actions, Scispot AI, Scibot, MCP, forms and portals, a workflow engine, Trust Vault , and dashboards. Scispot combines these capabilities inside one Digital Brain so the buyer does not have to assemble disconnected products. It can also keep an existing ELN, LIMS, SDMS, QMS, ERP, data lake, or customer-built system in place. That includes systems such as Benchling, Dotmatics, LabVantage, LabWare, and other third-party apps. What is ERP software for life sciences? What is a life sciences ERP? It is ERP software tailored for life sciences companies, including pharmaceutical, biotech and medical device companies, whose business processes face strict regulatory guidelines and require more documentation than a general commercial workflow. A life sciences ERP must track what happened, which version governed the work, which material lots were used, who reviewed the result, and how the final record connects to the source data. Pharmaceutical companies often need detailed recipe and formula documentation, Electronic Batch Records (EBRs), Master Batch Records (MBRs), and robust inventory controls. They also need lot or serial number tracking so teams can locate affected material quickly during a recall, deviation, investigation, or other correction. Medical device teams may need Device Master Record/Device History Record (DMR/DHR) controls that connect design specifications and production processes to the actual units, lots, inspections, results, and approvals. Scispot treats this scientific context as core ERP data. Samples, reagents, kits, consumables, equipment, lots, aliquots, plates, batches, protocols, test results, reports, storage locations, shipments, and approvals can live in one connected model. That makes Scispot a life sciences ERP for the work a general enterprise system does not model well. The distinction matters in practice. A finance ERP can show that a reagent was purchased. Scispot can show which lot was received, where it was stored, when it expires, which protocol consumed it, which sample and instrument run used it, whether the QC checks passed, who approved the result, and which report or COA went to the customer. That is the operating detail life science companies need to run faster and defend the record later. How Scispot functions as ERP software for life sciences Scispot manages the lab-side lifecycle of materials, samples, work, data, quality, and delivery. Labsheets act as structured master data for samples, reagents, compounds, kits, consumables, equipment, customers, projects, and jobs. Location Manager and Manifests map rooms, freezers, shelves, racks, boxes, plates, and well positions. Inventory Automation records quantity used and quantity left when a protocol or run consumes material. Labflows and Order Manager move work from intake through testing, review, reporting, and delivery. In practice, this is what an ERP for the lab should do. Scispot controls operational resources, tracks work in progress, records material issue to production, coordinates people and instruments, routes exceptions, and creates approved outputs. Labs can use it for research operations, regulated service delivery, diagnostics, quality testing, bioprocessing, and production-adjacent workflows. For many lab-centric organizations, this removes the need to buy a separate ERP for the lab floor. Scispot also works with the enterprise ERP. A NetSuite integration can sync Purchase Orders, Item Receipts, Vendor Bills, Locations, and Job records. Lab consumption can flow back to a project or client job for cost allocation, assay billing, or finance charge-back. SAP and ERP integrations can connect sample-to-product traceability, manufacturing context, inventory movements, and quality status. QuickBooks can receive purchasing and inventory data without duplicate data entry. The same pattern applies to Odoo, Microsoft Dynamics 365, Salesforce, monday.com, Quartzy, FreezerPro, Semble, CTMS tools, warehouse systems, and other business apps. For a CRO or service lab, Scispot can also run the order loop. An order enters through a form, portal, CRM, or connected billing event. Scispot registers the samples, assigns tests, applies QC holds, routes review, generates the report or COA, and shows status to the customer. Invoicing can stay in the finance system while Scispot runs the work that earns the revenue. Early-stage and lab-centric companies can use Scispot as their operations ERP. Larger organizations can use it as the lab ERP beside the corporate ERP. In both cases, Scispot remains the source for scientific truth and lab execution while the finance platform can continue to own general ledger, payroll, tax, and enterprise-wide Accounting, AR and AP. Managed Lab Brain Ops can then keep the integrations, rules, dashboards, and evidence healthy as the lab changes. Key features of ERP software for life sciences Key features of a life sciences ERP start with the standard ERP applications that every business needs, including manufacturing management, accounting and purchasing. Life sciences operations also need scientific records, traceability, quality controls, and regulated evidence that general life science ERP systems often leave to separate tools. ‍ ‍ ‍ Batch Records Both international and country-specific rules require life science manufacturers to control how products are made. Current Good Manufacturing Practice (cGMP) requires documentation that shows the approved process was followed and the correct inputs were used during each step of production. Batch Records create that evidence. EBRs show what happened during execution, while MBRs define the approved master process or master recipe. The ability to create and capture EBRs and MBRs electronically removes paper batch record forms and reduces repeated transcription. ERP software with batch record capabilities should connect instructions, materials, execution, checks, exceptions, review, and release in one seamless workflow. That improves efficiency, reduces errors, increases productivity, and strengthens traceability across compliance tasks. Scispot supports this model through versioned protocols, Labspaces, Labsheets, Inventory Automation, Activity Logs, Page Signing, reviewer approval, QC gates, and controlled reporting. A batch or work order can link the material lots consumed, equipment used, process data, calculations, deviations, signatures, and release output. For formal regulated use, Scispot can be configured and validated for the customer's intended use, with Trust Vault holding the related evidence. Device Master Record/Device History Record (DMR/DHR) Device Master Record/Device History Record (DMR/DHR) workflows play a similar role in medical device development and production. A DMR defines how a device should be made. A DHR shows what happened for a specific lot, unit, or production run and provides evidence that the approved instructions were followed. Scispot can configure DMR and DHR records by linking controlled specifications, methods, bills of material, work steps, material lots, test results, inspections, deviations, approvals, and final reports. The result is simplified traceability across product design, inventory and bill of materials management, manufacturing evidence, and regulatory requirements. Lot and serial traceability Lot and serial traceability is basic ERP work in life sciences, but it becomes much more useful when it connects to the lab record. Scispot can generate or manage unique identifiers, barcodes, lots, serials, aliquots, derivatives, plates, and parent-child sample relationships. Teams can trace a result back through the run, sample, material, supplier lot, location, and receipt record. This makes a recall or investigation faster because the team can identify affected material and downstream records without rebuilding the chain from spreadsheets. It also supports trend analysis because lot performance, test outcomes, deviations, and consumption history remain connected. Barcoding and scanning Barcoding and scanning reduce manual data entry at receiving, storage, movement, use, and disposal. ERP barcoding capabilities can also track equipment, labor and jobs. Scispot supports barcode print and scan flows for samples, reagents, kits, storage positions, boxes, plates, and work records, which reduces human error and produces more accurate data. A received item can be scanned, assigned to a freezer, rack, box, or well, and linked to its lot, expiry, supplier, and purchase context. A scientist can scan material into a protocol run, so the quantity updates automatically and the record keeps the exact lot used. Advanced inventory controls Life sciences operations have inventory needs that generic systems often miss. Materials may have strict material expiration dates, refrigerated goods, frozen or cryogenic storage, quarantine states, preparation dates, parent-child relationships, and method-specific eligibility rules. Scispot provides Advanced inventory controls and lab inventory management that track quantity, quantity consumed, quantity left, unit, Price Per Unit, lot, expiry, status, owner, and location. This gives labs practical Inventory Control tied to real work. Teams can optimize stock levels, track locations, automate reorders, capture data in real time, and forecast future inventory needs using actual lab consumption rather than rough purchasing history. Custom thresholds can trigger low-stock alerts. Expiry rules can flag material before use. Equipment maintenance or calibration status can block or route work. Automated replenishment workflows can notify a buyer or create a purchase request. These are practical Material Resource Planning (MRP) signals for the lab, connected to the work that creates demand. Bill of Materials (BOM) management Bill of Materials (BOM) management defines the parts, materials, and steps required to create a product, including subassemblies. Life sciences companies also need to preserve the method, lot, quantity, condition, and result associated with those inputs. Scispot supports BOM-like structures through versioned protocol templates, material registries, parent-child relationships, Inventory Automation, generated materials, batch records, and work instructions. It can record what should be used and what was actually used, which is often more valuable to the lab than a static list. Some organizations need formal single- or multi-level BOMs or Bill of Materials with unlimited revisions in an established manufacturing ERP. Scispot can connect to that system while maintaining the live lab-side recipe, sample and material lineage, consumption, yield, QC status, and approved result. This keeps the financial and manufacturing master aligned with actual scientific execution. ‍ ‍ Supplier management Life science companies remain responsible for supplier-provided material and services. Supplier management needs a complete view of supplier interaction, material, terms, pricing and supplier performance, along with the lot, receipt, inspection, storage, use, and quality history of each item. Scispot handles the operational side of supplier management, giving life science ERP systems the lab detail they usually lack. It can capture supplier and item records, lot and receipt data, certificates, attachments, inspection status, storage location, use history, and quality events. Through ERP integration, procurement teams can retain the formal buy-and-pay process while Scispot becomes the request and usage system of record. Inspections ERP inspection applications confirm that received or produced goods meet established standards. Scispot can route incoming, in-process, and final inspections through defined checks, required fields, acceptance criteria, QC holds, exceptions, and approval paths. The record stays linked to the item, lot, sample, batch, method, and result. This approach creates automated records for compliance and traceability. A failed check can flag, block, route, and document the issue instead of allowing the work to move forward without context. Electronic signature approval capabilities Electronic signature approval capabilities should do more than place a name on a PDF. They should connect identity, date and time, meaning, record state, approval workflow, and audit evidence. Electronic signature capabilities in Scispot can include authenticated signing, role controls, reviewer approval, page signing, time-stamped activity, and controlled outputs. Trust Vault keeps approval evidence, audit records, validation material, and recurring compliance artifacts connected to the workflow. Scispot supports ALCOA+ data integrity and can be configured for 21 CFR Part 11-controlled workflows. The customer's quality system still owns intended use, procedures, validation decisions, and regulated approvals. Real-time data and reporting across the lab A life sciences ERP should provide Real-time data and reporting across inventory, samples, orders, projects, instruments, testing, QC, reports, and customer delivery. Scispot dashboards can show inventory levels, work in progress, turnaround time, review queues, QC flags, resource utilization, man-hours, lead times, and KPIs. Managers can see where work is blocked instead of asking each team for a status update. Because Scispot connects the operating record, reports can use the same approved data that scientists and reviewers used. Controlled templates can generate reports, COAs, sample summary forms, and customer outputs without retyping results. Cross-run analytics can compare methods, instruments, lots, batches, or projects. GLUE and controlled APIs can send structured data to data lakes, bioinformatics, analytics, and AI systems with source lineage intact. This is the ERP reporting and planning layer for science operations. It gives finance better consumption and cost data, gives lab leaders operational visibility, gives Quality the evidence trail, and gives data teams governed context instead of isolated files. What are the benefits of ERP software for life sciences? Benefits of ERP software for life sciences start with operational efficiency. ERP software brings daily work into one system and reduces time-consuming, error-prone manual input across inventory, samples, testing, quality, reporting, and finance. ‍ ‍ Improved productivity ERP systems improve productivity by automating routine work and reducing manual data entry. Scispot removes file movement, repeated sample registration, result transcription, inventory reconciliation, status chasing, and report assembly. The practical gain is not just fewer clicks. It is more samples, runs, studies, or client reports handled by the same team. Greater innovation Greater innovation comes from making trusted data easy to find, compare, and reuse. Scispot connects experiments, protocols, samples, instrument outputs, calculations, decisions, and outcomes, so teams can use real-time data for informed decision-making and strategic planning. This helps scientists identify trends, reuse prior work, streamline product development, and innovate faster. Easier regulatory compliance Easier regulatory compliance depends on accurate record-keeping, clear ownership, controlled workflows, and evidence created during normal work. Many ERP systems advertise built-in compliance features, automating reporting, and built-in audit trails. In regulated life sciences, those controls must also connect to the scientific event that produced the record. Simplified collaboration Simplified collaboration comes from one shared operating record across departments and locations. Scispot also supports customer and partner portals, forms, notifications, and connected project management. Stronger data security Stronger data security requires centralized data storage, robust security protocols, controlled access, and a clear record of who viewed or changed critical information. Scispot uses role-based permissions and enterprise identity options so only authorized personnel can access defined records and actions. Controls such as secure cloud storage, advanced encryption, audit logging, backups, and regular updates help protect data and reduce exposure to emerging threats. Security evidence and compliance records can be maintained through Trust Vault and the customer's controlled review process. Cost savings Cost savings come from lower manual effort, fewer errors, less rework, better inventory use, faster reporting, and fewer disconnected tools. Streamlining processes lowers operational costs because teams spend less time on duplicate data entry and reconciliation. Integrated applications also improve visibility into all business processes, which helps leaders optimize resources and reduce waste. Scispot can reduce the need for separate lab inventory, workflow, sample tracking, reporting, portal, and lightweight manufacturing tools, while still connecting to the corporate systems that should remain. ‍ How Scispot connects lab operations with finance and procurement A general ERP is strong at enterprise purchasing and money. Scispot is strong at the lab work that creates demand, consumes materials, generates results, and produces billable or releasable outputs. The two systems can sync bidirectionally. ‍ Scispot is the most intuitive LIMS++ , offering seamless sample tracking, compliance automation, and AI-driven insights for modern labs. ‍ A purchase flow can begin with a low-stock signal or purchase request in Scispot. Validation and regulated operations Life sciences buyers often ask whether an ERP platform is fully validated. title: From PDFs to Possibilities
summary: Welcoming product visionary Jillian Hale as we build a modular, dynamic future for research. Jillian’s background spans product strategy, communication, and platform design. She brings a unique blend of user-centered thinking and a deep respect for how scientific work gets done.
body_text: From PDFs to Possibilities Curvenote’s Mission to Modernize Scientific Communication Rowan Cockett · Welcoming product visionary Jillian Hale as we build a modular, dynamic future for research. Meet our Curvenote Leadership Team Where’s that figure from the microscopy talk last month? If you’ve worked in a lab, you’ve probably asked (or been asked) that question. Science is full of breakthrough ideas, but they’re often scattered across drives, buried in slide decks, or locked away in PDFs that no one can easily search or reuse. At Curvenote, we believe that the future of science shouldn’t be stuck in outdated systems designed for the printing press. Research deserves tools that match the way scientists work today: collaboratively, iteratively, and online. We’re building a platform that turns static outputs into dynamic, modular, and reusable building blocks of knowledge. This fall, we’re preparing to launch a major evolution of the Curvenote platform, and we’re thrilled to welcome Jillian Hale as our new Product Lead to help shape this future. Why Jillian Joined Curvenote ¶ Jillian’s background spans product strategy, communication, and platform design. She brings a unique blend of user-centered thinking and a deep respect for how scientific work gets done. “Since completing my own graduate studies over a decade ago, I realized publishing formats haven’t really changed,” she says. “Despite all the digital tools we have, science is still formatted for print, and that doesn’t do justice to how visual, interactive, and collaborative research really is.” Jillian Hale joins Curvenote as a Product Lead. Before joining Curvenote, Jillian was building platforms that helped tourism operators punch above their weight, reaching global audiences and creating meaningful connections. She sees the same opportunity in science: researchers with world-changing discoveries, stuck using legacy tools that weren’t built for collaboration, modularity, or the speed of modern research. “Science is full of brilliant findings, but they’re often locked away in PDFs or buried in file systems,” Jillian explains. “We need to make that knowledge easier to access, reuse, and connect, both inside and outside the lab.” The Challenge Researchers Face Today ¶ Across the research ecosystem, a common set of problems keeps showing up. Researchers struggle to find content they know exists, especially when it’s stored in different places or lacks clear context. New lab members often can’t get up to speed quickly because there’s no central, searchable system for presentations, methods, or past work. Even basic elements like figures and equations can be hard to retrieve or reuse without a lot of manual effort. And while research is inherently modular—built from methods, data, code, and results—the current systems treat it as one long document. This slows down collaboration and makes sharing knowledge harder than it should be. A Modular Future for Science ¶ Curvenote is building for a future where research outputs are modular, searchable, and alive. Instead of treating a paper as a final destination, our platform helps researchers manage the core components—like figures, methods, and code snippets—as reusable pieces that can be pulled into any format, from slides to manuscripts. With a relentless focus on researcher experience, Curvenote is pioneering tools that turn every piece of scientific work into a reusable, interconnected building block—transforming how knowledge flows across labs, collaborators, and the world. “Think of it like building with Lego,” Jillian says. “Your research isn’t just one big block. It’s made up of smaller parts you can remix, share, and reuse. It should be as easy to pull a figure into your slide deck as it is to post an image on social media.” This shift makes it easier for labs to stay organized, for researchers to discover relevant work, and for collaborators to move quickly across evolving projects. What’s Coming This Fall ¶ We’re gearing up to launch Curvenote’s next-generation platform this September, relentlessly enhancing our tools to lead the future of open science with greater adaptability than ever before. We’re giving you smarter ways to organize, search, and reuse research content. You’ll be able to reuse figures or results directly into other outputs without reinventing the wheel every time. We’re also deepening integration with tools researchers already use, including Jupyter and MyST, to create a seamless experience across writing, presenting, and publishing. “Scientists shouldn’t have to jump through hoops to reuse their own work. I want a world where grabbing a figure for a talk or a grant is as easy as dragging and dropping it into place.” Follow along for what’s coming next and get ready to experience a more modular, dynamic future for scientific communication. title: National Grid launches consultation to help shape £30m community fund for Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex
summary: National Grid is inviting communities across Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex to help shape how community funding linked to the proposed Norwich to Tilbury project could be delivered should the project receive development consent.
body_text: National Grid launches consultation to help shape £30m community fund for Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex Home 8th July 2026 Press release Funding worth more than £30 million could support projects across Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex, delivering lasting benefits for communities hosting new electricity infrastructure. Residents, businesses and community organisations invited to help shape how community funding linked to Norwich to Tilbury could be used. Residents invited to take part in two webinars to learn more about the fund and how to have your say. National Grid is inviting communities across Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex to help shape how community funding linked to the proposed Norwich to Tilbury project could be delivered should the project receive development consent. A survey has been launched marking the start of a programme of engagement designed to ensure people have a say in funding priorities, helping to shape a fund that reflects what matters most to people locally. In line with Government guidance on community funds for new electricity transmission infrastructure, Norwich to Tilbury is expected to provide over £30 million in funding for communities across the region. National Grid is now seeking feedback from residents, businesses, community groups and local organisations on the issues that matter most to them and where they believe funding could make the biggest difference. Potential areas for investment could include improving community facilities, enhancing green spaces, supporting skills and employment opportunities, and initiatives that improve physical and mental wellbeing. To help people learn more about the proposed fund and how to help shape it, National Grid is holding two online webinars on 22 July from 6pm to 7pm and 29 July from 12pm to 1pm. The sessions will provide an overview of the proposed community fund programme and give participants the chance to ask questions. Simon Pepper, Project Director for Norwich to Tilbury, said: "Norwich to Tilbury is a project that would play a vital role in strengthening the electricity network and supporting the UK's transition to cleaner, more secure, home-grown energy. We believe communities hosting this infrastructure should also share in its benefits for years to come." "Over the coming months, we will be giving people across Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex an opportunity to influence how the community fund could support the places where they live and work, starting with the survey we are launching today. We want to hear directly from local people about where this funding could make the greatest difference and leave a lasting positive impact." Emma Turner, Head of Socioeconomic and Community Benefits, said: "This is an important opportunity to ensure major energy infrastructure projects deliver lasting benefits for the areas that host them. We’re working closely with communities and stakeholders to help ensure this funding supports projects that make a real difference locally and create a lasting positive impact across the region." "By understanding local priorities, we can help ensure funding supports projects that reflect community needs and deliver meaningful outcomes for local people." The fund will be delivered in two parts: a local fund providing grants to local projects and causes, and a strategic fund, designed to support broader regional priorities. This approach is intended to ensure funding priorities are shaped by local feedback, with transparent decision-making and independent oversight of how funding is allocated. The funding would become available if the project receives development consent and construction begins. Residents, community organisations and businesses can take part in the survey by visiting https://www.nationalgrid.com/electricity-transmission/network-and-infrastructure/infrastructure-projects/norwich-to-tilbury. The survey is the first stage of engagement to help shape the community fund, with further opportunities for communities to provide feedback planned after the project’s planning examination has closed.

body_text: WESTMINSTER, Colo.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Jul. 16, 2026-- TriSalus Life Sciences, Inc. (Nasdaq: TLSI) (the “Company”), an oncology company integrating novel delivery technology with standard-of-care therapies and an investigational immunotherapeutic to transform outcomes for patients with solid tumors, today announced that it will host a conference call and webcast on Thursday, August 6, 2026 at 4:30 PM eastern time to discuss its financial results for the quarter ended June 30, 2026. A press release detailing the results will be issued prior to the call. Parties interested in participating by phone should register using this online form . After registering for the call, dial-in details will be provided in an auto-generated email containing a link to the conference phone number along with a PIN. The event will also be webcast live on the investor relations section of TriSalus’ website. A replay will also be available on the website following the event. About TriSalus Life Sciences TriSalus Life Sciences® is an oncology focused medical technology company seeking to transform outcomes for patients with solid tumors by integrating its innovative delivery technology with standard-of-care therapies, and with its investigational immunotherapeutic, nelitolimod, a class C Toll-like receptor 9 agonist, for a range of different therapeutic and technology applications. The Company’s platform includes devices that utilize a proprietary drug delivery technology and a clinical stage investigational immunotherapy. The Company’s three FDA-cleared devices use its proprietary Pressure-Enabled Drug Delivery™ (PEDD) approach to deliver a range of therapeutics: the TriNav® Infusion System and TriNav Infusion System LV for hepatic arterial infusion of liver tumors and the Pancreatic Retrograde Venous Infusion System for pancreatic tumors. The PEDD technology is a novel delivery approach designed to address the anatomic limitations of arterial infusion for the pancreas. The PEDD approach modulates pressure and flow in a manner that delivers more therapeutic to the tumor and is designed to reduce undesired delivery to normal tissue, bringing the potential to improve patient outcomes. Nelitolimod, the Company’s investigational immunotherapeutic candidate, is designed to improve patient outcomes by treating the immunosuppressive environment created by many tumors and which can make current immunotherapies ineffective in the liver and pancreas. Patient data generated during Pressure-Enabled Regional Immuno-Oncology™ (PERIO) clinical trials support the hypothesis that nelitolimod delivered via the PEDD technology may have favorable immune effects within the liver and systemically. The target for nelitolimod, TLR9, is expressed across cancer types and the mechanical barriers addressed by the PEDD technology are commonly present as well. The Company is in the final stages of data completion for a number of phase 1 clinical trials and will begin exploring partnership opportunities for development. title: A Comprehensive Guide to Sleeping Pill Side Effects
summary: Discover the potential side effects of sleeping pills. Our comprehensive guide covers risks, benefits, and alternatives to ensure a good night's sleep.
body_text: We asked Dr. Shiyan Yeo, Internal Medicine Physician, Sleep Medicine Expert about sleeping pills and its potential risks. She says: “Most sleep medications were never designed for long-term use. It’s critical to understand the risks, especially dependency and cognitive effects.” Ultimately, sleeping medications should be used, if at all, in the short-term. If you'r struggling with sleep, you deserve to know what you're really getting into with sleeping pills before you start. Understanding the downsides is the first step to finding a solution that actually lasts. Let's break down what these medications do, the risks they carry, and how you can find a better way to get the rest you need. Ready to skip the pills and find a real solution? Our program, Sleep Reset, helps you fix the root causes of your sleep issues - just take our free sleep quiz! Understanding Sleeping Pills At their core, sleeping pills are sedatives. They work by changing your brain chemistry to make you drowsy. How Do Sleeping Pills Work? Most common prescription pills, like Ambien or Lunesta, work by boosting a natural chemical in your brain called GABA. Think of GABA as a dimmer switch, it calms down brain activity, quieting the "noise" that keeps you awake. Older medications, called benzodiazepines, do this too, but they have a wider range of effects and a higher risk of dependency. Doctors usually prescribe these as a short-term tool when insomnia is severe and nothing else has worked. They are meant to be a temporary bridge, not a permanent solution. Influence on GABA, a neurotransmitter that slows down brain activity Promotion of melatonin release to regulate sleep-wake cycles Inhibition of serotonin and norepinephrine to decrease alertness Activation of the brain's natural sleep systems Common Types of Sleeping Pills Delving into the world of sleeping pills , we primarily encounter two categories: Benzodiazepines and Non-benzodiazepines. Both function to promote sleep but differ in their effects and side effects . Understanding Benzodiazepines: These are older generation medications including flurazepam, temazepam, and triazolam, renowned for their sedative, anti-anxiety, anticonvulsant, and muscle relaxing properties. However, they also carry a higher risk of dependency and withdrawal. Getting to Know Non-Benzodiazepines: Known as 'Z-drugs', they comprise newer medications such as zolpidem, zaleplon, and eszopiclone. These have a shorter half-life and fewer side effects, making them a preferred choice for many patients and physicians. Unpacking Zolpidem: Often marketed as Ambien, this is a common short-term treatment prescribed for insomnia. It works by slowing brain activity, allowing for sleep, but can also cause memory loss and abnormal behavior if misused or taken in excess. Exploring Eszopiclone: Sold under the brand name Lunesta, this is another widely used sleeping aid, approved for long-term use. While it can effectively treat insomnia, dependency and withdrawal symptoms can occur when discontinued abruptly. When Are Sleeping Pills Prescribed? Primarily, sleeping pills are prescribed when lifestyle adjustments and non-medicated treatment strategies have failed to improve chronic insomnia or sleep disorders. Patients battling chronic insomnia for a lengthy period. Individuals who have failed to respond adequately to cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I). Persons suffering from sleep disorders like sleep apnea. Patients whose daily life functioning is adversely affected due to lack of quality sleep. Individuals who suffer from frequent night wakings or difficulty falling asleep. Risks Associated with Sleeping Pills The promise of a good night's sleep is tempting, but that relief can come at a cost. Here are the most common side effects people experience: Alterations in mental and physical functioning Increments on dependence and increased risk of addiction Potential increase in mortality rate Development of tolerance leading to increased dosage Potential for severe withdrawal symptoms Increased risk of falls and accidents Potential Side Effects of Sleeping Pills It’s tempting to think of a sleeping pill as a simple fix, but it's important to know you're often getting more than just a good night's rest. The price for that sleep can be high, with side effects like an upset stomach, dizziness, memory lapses, and a real risk of becoming dependent. ‍ Drowsiness and Daytime Sleepiness Ever take something for sleep and feel like you're moving through fog the next day? That’s the most common side effect. The sedative effect can linger long after you wake up, leaving you drowsy, a step behind mentally, and even a bit clumsy or uncoordinated. This can make driving or focusing at work genuinely difficult and unsafe. Have you noticed an unusual level of drowsiness since starting your sleeping pill regimen? This is a common side effect experienced by many users. It can affect your ability to perform daily tasks safely and efficiently. The intensity of drowsiness can vary greatly among individuals and is influenced by factors such as the type and dosage of the medication, your individual metabolism, and your overall health status. An adjustment to your sleeping pill regimen may be necessary to manage daytime sleepiness effectively. Nausea and Upset Stomach An unquiet belly can underscore your restful slumber. Prescription sleeping pills might be the source if you're often unsteady and queasy after use. Not everyone experiences this, but it's crucial to be cognisant of these common indicators. Nausea isn't an idyllic way to welcome your waking hours. Sleeping pills, though effective, may exact a toll on your digestive system, causing an upset stomach as your body adjusts to the medication. Be extra mindful if consuming food triggers discomfort along with your prescription. An upset stomach carries the potential to negatively affect your overall well-being, placing additional mental strain that could further entertain your insomnia. Headaches Some individuals may experience headaches after consuming sleeping pills, a frequent side effect of these medications. The intensity of these headaches might vary, potentially disrupting your routine. If you're undergoing headache woes and insomnia, you might inadvertently blame the wrong condition. The medication prescribed to alleviate your sleep issues may, paradoxically, be causing distressing headaches. Understanding the relationship between your medication and headaches is crucial. Consulting with your doctor or pharmacist can empower you to make informed decisions about your health and the potential side effects of sleeping pills. Memory Problems This one can be unsettling. Sleeping pills can interfere with your brain’s ability to store memories while you sleep. You might have trouble remembering things you did right before bed, or just feel a general sense of forgetfulness the next day. It’s not just a long-term risk; it can happen even after a single use. Memory problems sit amongst a multitude of potential side effects incurred from sleeping pill usage. As such, the 'hidden cost' of these medications may involve memory impairments or even amnesia, raising concerns about their long-term implications on cognitive health. Sleeping pills work by slowing brain activity, in turn, facilitating sleep. Yet, this calming effect can persist into the waking hours, clouding memory. This 'hangover effect' may often include temporary forgetfulness and trouble concentrating. Distinctly, scenarios like not remembering activities performed right before bedtime (while the medication is taking effect) can occur. This 'anterograde amnesia' means new information isn't successfully transitioned from short-term to long-term memory while under the influence. A common misconception is that memory issues only surface with prolonged sleeping pill use. However, even sporadic use can result in noticeable memory impairments, casting doubt on the notion of safe, occasional use. Lastly, it is crucial not to ignore these memory issues. If experienced, it's recommended to consult your healthcare provider promptly. It might indicate a need to adjust the dosage, change the medication, or explore alternative treatments. Dizziness and Lack of Coordination A surging wave of unsteadiness often follows in the wake of sleeping pill ingestion - dizziness may become your unwelcome companion. Rooted in the pill’s function of slowing brain activity, this symptom can create a disorienting detachment from reality. Staggering, clumsiness, or the sensation of the room spinning aren’t eerie horror movie effects; they could be side effects of your sleeping pills. This lack of coordination, while seldom serious, may lead to potentially hazardous situations, such as falling or stumbling. Slipping into a tranquil sleep is the allure of sleeping pills, but navigating in a foggy haze afterwards is the less advertised downside. The drowsy after-effects of these medications can impair your daily functioning, by causing dizziness and loss of balance. Moving through your day shouldn't feel like traversing uncertain ground, yet that's the reality for some who use sleeping pills. These drugs can induce unsteadiness, further bolstering the argument for careful, monitored usage of sleep-inducing medications. If you relate to feeling like a wobbly sailor after a storm, your sleeping pills could be the silent culprits. Side effects such as dizziness and impaired coordination aren’t to be ignored; prompt discussion with your healthcare professional is paramount. Changes in Appetite Sleeping pills can unexpectedly alter your eating habits. Some individuals may experience increased cravings, while others may suffer from a diminished interest in food. It's crucial to recognize these changes as potential side effects to manage them effectively. A paradoxical effect induced by sleeping pills is the sudden onset of food cravings or aversions. You might develop an appetite for foods you usually avoid or find your favorite dishes unappealing. This can complicate dietary habits and even nutritional intake. These alterations in appetite may be short-lived or persistent, varying from one individual to another. Therefore, monitoring such changes when starting on sleeping pills is crucial. Should they occur, consider discussing them with your healthcare provider to devise a suitable coping strategy. Dependence and Addiction This is the biggest risk. Your body gets used to the medication surprisingly quickly. Soon, the dose that worked last week doesn't work anymore, so you take more. This cycle is called tolerance, and it can quickly lead to dependence, where you feel like you can't sleep without the pill. Getting off them can be incredibly difficult and can cause withdrawal symptoms, including even worse insomnia. Repeated use for extended periods creates tolerance and can potentially propel users into the clutches of addiction. Essentially, individuals may find themselves unable to function normally without the medication, causing severe sleep disruptions when attempted to cease. The subtle transition from aiding sleep to creating addiction characterizes the dark side of sleeping pills. For many, what started as a solution ends up as another problem to overcome. Sleeping pills should never be viewed as a long-term solution to sleep struggles. Without proper medical guidance, the risk of slipping from use to abuse increases substantially, highlighting the importance of professional oversight during treatment. The therapeutic use of sleeping pills requires strict adherence to prescribed doses. Any deviation from the prescribed regimen can trigger a cascading cycle of dependence and addiction. Utilizing sleeping pills as a crutch and not a treatment tool blurs the line between therapeutic use and substance abuse. Sexual Dysfunction Sleeping pills might potentially alter your sexual performance, often posing a blow to intimacy. Temporary sexual disorders including decreased libido, erectile dysfunction in men, and lower vaginal lubrication in women have been observed. Closer examination reveals that sleeping pills can impact your sex life, transforming desire into dysfunction. Depression, a common side-effect of these medications, could contribute indirectly to a reduced sex drive. The consequence of long-term use of sleeping pills can extend beyond sleep-related issues to affect intimate relationships. It's crucial to consider these potential implications and discuss them with your doctor before initiating treatment. Allergic Reactions Allergic reactions to sleeping pills could present as skin-related issues, such as a sudden, unexplained rash, hives, or itching. These reactions, while unpleasant, unequivocally signal an intolerance towards the medication critical to address immediately. If you are facing symptoms such as itching, rash, or hives after taking sleeping pills, consider them as possible allergic reactions. Act promptly as these symptoms should never be ignored and require immediate consultation with a medical professional. Talking to Your Doctor If you're taking sleeping pills and experiencing any of these side effects, talk to your doctor. They can help you create a plan to reduce your dose safely. Never stop taking them cold turkey. To open this imperative conversation, start with your concerns about taking sleeping pills. Explain your sleep habits, health history, and lifestyle factors impacting your insomnia. Remember, valuable insights can be obtained from this discussion. It aids your doctor to comprehend your unique circumstances and prescribe the most suitable treatment plan, keeping potential side effects in mind. Exploring Alternative Treatment Options For a true, long-term solution, you have to address the reason you're not sleeping in the first place. Lifestyle changes like maintaining a sleep schedule, practicing good sleep hygiene, and creating a restful environment can make a significant difference. These alterations may negate the need for medication. This is where behavioral therapy comes in. As Clinical Psychologist Dr. Suzanne Gorovoy puts it: “Behavioral approaches like CBT-I treat the root causes of insomnia, without the potential side effects of sedative medications.” Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) is considered the gold standard for treating chronic insomnia. It's a drug-free approach that helps you retrain your brain and body for natural, healthy sleep. Diet and exercise also play crucial roles. Certain foods can induce quality sleep, while regular physical activity can enhance sleep duration and quality. Engaging with these alternatives could make sleeping pills unnecessary. We use CBT-I principles to help you fall asleep and stay asleep all night. There are no quick fixes here, just a science-backed plan to help you fall asleep, stay asleep, and wake up feeling like yourself again. You'll even get a dedicated sleep coach to guide and support you through daily texts. Our program does not rely on harmful pills, melatonin or supplements – which means no grogginess, dependency, or long-term health risks. It all starts with understanding your own sleep. The Sleep Reset program is available on iOS and Android. Take the Sleep quiz now. Take our Sleep Calculator and Chronotype Quiz to learn more about your sleep personality! title: First Principles Thinking: Capital Partners
